utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Slobodan Tusevljak lived and worked in Sarajevo until the war broke out. He testifies about the deterioration of interethnic relations in the city, the loss of job from his company, and the fact that until May 1992 he was not recruited militarily nor did he have any weapons. On the 8th of June, 1992, Muslim units attacked his settlement and pushed back the locals and their guards some 200 to 250 metres to the rear, killed five to six men, and wounded about ten people and then torched their houses. After this attack, a new defence line was established which remained undisturbed until the end of the war because his units engaged only in defensive operations defending their positions. In this unit, the witness was a platoon commander of a platoon That belonged to the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. The position of his platoon was of great strategic importance because he secured the road Lukavica-Pale. Throughout the war they were under intense artillery, infantry, and sniper fire and a lot of soldiers and civilians in the rear of his unit were killed. According to official information, during the war at this position - especially in Ozren Street - 230 soldiers were killed and scores of civilians. The fire was opened from civilian areas and the command of the opposing unit was at the Hrasno Brdo MZ. Never throughout the war did he receive from the superior command any oral or written orders to open fire on civilian targets nor did he issue such orders to his men. The witness specifically comments on the sniping incident marked As F4 in the indictment and claims that during this incident there were no snipers in his unit and precisely so that in order to avoid the sniping of the other side of their positions they erected screens of various kinds at the most sensitive portions of the separation line. And finally, this witness will speak about his knowledge about the supply of parts of Sarajevo that was under the control of the BH Army, the supply of electricity, water, and gas to these areas.

utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we take the break now. You get organised. At this moment that's D539 and D540. We'll not spend any time on any statement which is not uploaded into e-court which is not assigned a number because it's non-existent for us. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will do so. After the break, we'll inform you thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you have 20 minutes to put questions to the witness. You wasted now more than half an hour. We'll nevertheless not cut you short on the 20 minutes, but again that we are not amused is the soft language. We take a break after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stojanovic, I take it that you're now fully on top of the various versions of the various statements by the witness. Can we agree that whenever you refer to any statement that you refer to that statement by the number of paragraphs contained in that statement. We have the 26-paragraph statement which was attached to -- I think it was to the reply of the 92 ter filing; we have the 28-paragraph statement which is found in e-court under number D540; and we have a 13-paragraph statement which is in e-court as D539. If you use this system, unless you have a fourth or a fifth or a sixth version of whatever statement, if you use this reference there should be no confusion. Clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear, Your Honours. And if you allow, I would like to address in a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I err, please let me know. In keeping with instructions that I received from you that I should decide which one of the statements from the Karadzic case I will use, in the Veljevic case, we contacted the Prosecutor regarding this issue that has to do with the statements because there are two statements in the Karadzic case. And we agreed, and Mr. Shin will correct me if I'm mistaken, that the statement in this case - in the Karadzic case for this witness, D540, today, which was MFI'd - shall be the only statement from the Karadzic case that will be used here on the proviso that paragraph 25 of this statement should be redacted, the portion of the paragraph that deals with the F10 incident. In keeping with this agreement, we entered into e-court D540 and tendered it as an exhibit. Now a supplement to this statement, Your Honour, is what can be found at D539. And we are going to use, as agreed with the Prosecutor, one statement only in keeping with your instructions for the Veljevic case. So we will use only one statement from the Karadzic case which is the current D540. And with your leave, Your Honours, fully accepting that I may have caused confusion, I apologise, and I will now answer the question that Judge Fluegge put and also the question that Mr. Shin put to me. So please bear with me and use this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you do so, the version which is uploaded now in e-court as D540, the -- that should be redacted. But the one uploaded until now is a non-redacted version; is that clear? So we still are waiting for your redactions to be uploaded and then we'll decide --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on admission of what is now not even MFI'd but what is linked to reserved number D540. Okay. So we are still waiting for that. Please proceed. Now you're going to respond to Judge Fluegge's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, that's correct, Your Honours. The Honourable Judge Fluegge asked us where he can find in D540 support for the documents that we were tendering, and I will go in order. 1D02066 -- I apologise, 1D02066 corresponds to the Karadzic document, the Karadzic statement D540 in paragraph 8 of the D540 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have it on our screen. Oh, it is. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 540 of the Karadzic or is it 8547 of Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. It has the number 1D8547. With your leave, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. This seems to be correct. Madam Registrar has provisionally assigned number D541 to that. Any objection, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D541, which corresponds to 1D02066, although known under a different number in the Karadzic case, it being 1D8547, is admitted into evidence. Next one please, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document which in our case has the 65 ter number 1D02067 corresponds to document which in the statement D540 is mentioned in paragraph 9, 11, and 12, Your Honours. And in the Karadzic case it bears the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have it complete, Mr. Stojanovic. Any -- D542 was provisionally assigned to this document. Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Which means that 1D02067, known in the Karadzic case under 65 ter number 1D08548, is admitted into evidence as D542. Next one please, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document that we tendered, which in our case has the 65 ter number 1D02069, corresponds to document mentioned in this witness's statement D540 in paragraph 18 in the Karadzic case. It had the 65 ter number 1D8550.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's complete. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore 1D02069, known in the Karadzic case as 1D08550, is admitted under number D543. Next one Mr. Stojanovic. If you -- for the next ones, I think if you just refer to where we can find them and I have all the numbers so that we don't have to put it on the record twice. The next one is to be found where?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1 -- 1D02068, paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic please repeat the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the paragraph, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now 25 would be redacted. Will this also be redacted or not? No. I think this would not be redacted. Which means -- Mr. Shin, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just briefly. We won't take the position that it needs to be redacted, but we do note for the record that given the redaction that is forthcoming that the reference to F10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- on this exhibit is not associated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We do understand that and that's how we will deal with it. Therefore 1D02068, in the Karadzic case known as 1D08549, is admitted as D544. Mr. Stojanovic, the next one is to be found where?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 1D02070 and 1D02071 are mentioned in paragraph 27 of statement D540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, both documents have no English translation yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are names. If you think that that needs to be translated - it's a list because of the headings - then we suggest that these two documents are MFI'd for the time being until the translation is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at those exhibits. To start with, 1D02070. Could we have a -- is there no English version at all? If not, Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm told by Ms. Stewart that there is, in fact, an English version that has now been uploaded. I'm not sure at what point that was but is apparently available. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as always it's there. Yes. I see that the handwriting is copied from the original. It is the list of weapons of the 1st Platoon of the 4th Company and apparently gives numbers. And it seems that the English version is even giving more than what is found in the original I see, or does AP stand for "automatic rifle"? Is that how we have to understand it? And that M stands for "machine-gun" and that P -- AP stands for "semiautomatic rifle"? I take it that that's a -- yes. And I see that there is handwriting on it. Yes. Could we also have a look at the next one to see whether there is any English translation for 1D02071. Yes. There is now a translation for this one as well. Then no objections, Mr. Shin, against any of the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objections. We will take a look to see if there are any issues but that can be dealt with later. Any issues with the translation, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you provided the translations I take it that there should be no problem there. Mr. Stojanovic, 1D02070, also known in the Karadzic case as 65 ter 1D06090, is admitted into evidence as D545. 1D02071, in the Karadzic case known as 65 ter number 1D06091, is admitted into evidence as D546. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Shin --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the Prosecution's inquiry about this reference to an attack on a settlement still stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we would be happy to hear that when the witness is in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you had time to find in any of the three statements an attack on the 8th of June at the settlement the witness lived in, we'd like to hear where to find that. Mr. Stojanovic, you can't tell us where to find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm prepared to answer that question, but I understood you to mean that I could do it once the witness entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you make a summary of a statement of a witness, even without the witness you should be able to point at where it is to be found. So we'd like to hear from you now in which statement we find it, in what paragraph, before you put any further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. When we clarified this question regarding the documents, I wanted to indicate paragraph 9 of D540, the statement. Paragraph 9, could we please look at that in the electronic courtroom system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start from the second sentence in paragraph 9 where the witness said, and I would say I quoted it 90 per cent in my summary: "That day Muslims attacked our positions and pushed us back some 200 to 250 metres. First, they attacked us with the mortars and then ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue was whether positions were attacked, which is a rather military expression, or whether the settlement in which the witness lived was attacked. Mr. Shin told us that he had some doubts as to where to find a settlement to be attacked. If you can tell us, please tell us where that is found. If you can't tell us, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will tell you where I got that from. If we look at the next sentence when it's mentioned that it's the same event, from the lines: "... to which we had retreated we watched Muslims setting fire to our houses." That is his settlement. In his settlement they were setting fire to houses in this settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it's a -- more or less a summary of your interpretation of the middle of paragraph 9. Mr. Shin, shall we leave it to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to leave it to that. And, again, that paragraph does refer to a line of engagement and our positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and at the same time it also deals about burning down houses. Whether that's an attack or whether that is a follow-up of an attack is another matter. But we leave it to that. Mr. Stojanovic, you have got 20 minutes for any further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not use all of that time, Your Honours. I will be shorter. I hope that we have resolved some of the confusion. I think that we were in a situation where I wasn't even sure if I was clear about the paragraphs that I pointed out here. Could we now look at paragraph from D546, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the list of names, D546, Mr. Stojanovic, or did you want to refer to D5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's the document. I am just going to put a few questions regarding the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, are you able to remember whether throughout the entire period of the war there were members in your company who were not ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were Croats and Muslims from the beginning until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these all people who lived in the settlement that you held your lines in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at the list of these members of the 4th Company on the 18th of February, 1994, and are you able to tell us whether this was the company that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The number -- the name of the man next to number 6, Karlo, Bauer, what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And his family and his house, were they in the settlement where you had your front lines?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think that he was from Grbavica. But the rest of them were from that settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 73 there is Ivo Pejic, recorded as a member of your company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat. He was my neighbour. He lived on the lines. So his house was left below the line after the attack occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the attack on the 8th of June after you withdrew to new lines, what happened with his house?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It burned later. It was knocked down. Not just that house but all of those houses. There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak a bit louder so that the interpreters are better able to hear you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would now like to ask the witness to look at the name next to 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was also a member of your company, Dragan Pejic. What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat as well. He's the son of Ivo Pejic. That's his son. He was wounded then and then he went for medical treatment to Belgrade and after that he didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The name under 90, Himzo Sulejmanovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where his house was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not from our settlement. He was somewhere from the Grbavica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say Grbavica, how far is that from the positions where you were at?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps some 15 minutes by foot if you went along Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The name of the person next to number 96, Zrinko Sigel. What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat, also. I think that he lived with his mother in Grbavica, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally number 98, Petar Svalina, a member of your company. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat and my neighbour. He lived near my house. His house also burned down. It was torched on the 8th of June. His wife and her mother were in the house, they were captured, but they let his wife go. She came out of the house and then they torched it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to end with this question: You mentioned that about 230 members of your unit were killed during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to tell the Trial Chamber, do you have any information or any estimates as to how they died? What kind of fire were they killed by?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed in fighting. Most of them were killed in sniper fire. That street was exposed to sniper fire from the city and Asimovo Brdo. So it was mostly sniper fire but then shells and other things. The documentation remained and then after the signing of the Dayton Agreement, the documentation was left in that command. The territory fell under the federation authority. They found those documents with the list of all the fighters that were killed from the company. This number, 200-odd person, refers to the whole Ozrenska, not only my company but that street and other streets towards Grbavica. This is something I discussed with the commanders. This is not only the documentation for the company but there were also others who were not recorded in the -- this company but in their own companies as casualties, as people who were killed in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war as the platoon commander, did you have any crisis as a human being and did you have problems? Did you ever wish to leave this kind of position where there was fierce fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we frequently sought support because there were a lot of people, elderly people on this line who fought there and it was hard to hold this line. And then for about 15 days I left the lines because I just couldn't take it anymore. You know, I couldn't sleep, I couldn't rest, and anything. But then I returned later when the lines were manned with more personnel. It was improved a bit. So then we somehow continued, although these two were elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war did at any point -- your company commander was a company commander, a person of nonethnic Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a commander. He was a Croat. He was a major in the JNA. We put him as a commander because he was an active duty personnel. I believe he was a retired major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions and I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Shin to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber wonders what the relevance is of most of your questions over the last ten minutes. Casualties among soldiers. Is that a relevant issue in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in our view the relevant issues are the following: First, the fact that his unit was multiethnic through the war; Number two, the composition of his unit shows that these people fought for their homes and they fought near their houses and no one minded what ethnicity anybody else was; And that the victims of the BH Army in the killing and the fighting and the destruction of the homes were Serbs and Croats and Muslims. That was the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But I was asking for the relevance for this case. I mean, that there may have been non-Serbs in VRS units, is that relevant? They're a small minority. But is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the indictment that there was terror and that the -- there was an intent to terrorise the citizens of Sarajevo, we felt the need that we should point out here that the terrorising was not as it is presented in the indictment. It was terrorising of all the people who lived in Sarajevo who did not agree to the positions of the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities and not as it was presented here by other witnesses, and we would like to say here that the suffering was equal for everyone in Sarajevo, for Serbs, Bosnian Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I fully appreciate that Your Honours were putting questions to Mr. Stojanovic, but there may come a point where such colloquy should be held outside of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber is not convinced yet that what you tell us makes the issues really relevant. And especially in full respect for soldiers suffering sometimes fates which you would not wish anyone to undergo, that nevertheless a soldier being killed in war is not a crime. I mean, whether we like it or not. but that's a reality of war. And it looks as paying so much attention to soldiers having died may be based on a misunderstanding of what this case is really about. Let's move on. Mr. Shin, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Shin. Mr. Shin is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find him to your right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by making sure we understand what unit you were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think there may be something wrong with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We're back. I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I'd like to begin here by making sure we understand what unit you were in so there is no confusion. We'll start with your platoon. That was the 1st Platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you took over this platoon when Vito Kapuran was wounded?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When did that happen? What did you take over?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was in 1992 in the summer or thereabouts, after this attack on the 12th. It was either in July or in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now your rank was a private; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But then later I became a -- I was promoted to junior-lieutenant as a commander of this platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, does that mean that you became a junior-lieutenant in the summer of 1992 when you say you became platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that's a rank you held until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I returned that rank, if I may put it that way, when the time came when I just couldn't bear it there anymore, when we didn't have support and no personnel on that line, and then I was just a simple private. I believe this was in late 1993 or 1994. I tend to believe it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now in the Karadzic case you testified that Vito Kapuran was an activist in the local commune; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was this the same person as the Vito you mentioned in your Karadzic statement, paragraph 7, as a person who distributed small arms to Serbs prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the same person, Vito Kapuran.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In your Karadzic testimony, you were asked about the organisation of people in Lukavica, and the provision of weapons, you said, was done through the Crisis Staff. You stand by that; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vito was the activist, an activist of sorts, and they obtained these weapons somehow and then they distributed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in your Karadzic statement in paragraph 13, you say that - and we've heard that here - your platoon was part of the 4th Company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we've heard also that it was part of the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And your brigade was the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Actually, in 1992 wasn't the 4th Company part of a battalion that was designated the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was some kind of reorganisation later on, but I know that 1st -- later it became the 1st Platoon of the 4th Company, but then later that changed something per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's be clear here because we're going to be looking at documents. We want to avoid confusion. Throughout the war, you were in the 1st platoon except when you stepped down. Throughout the war you were in the 4th Company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, the 4th Company was part of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade and at some point it became the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Smbr; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the beginning of the war it was the latter, what you mentioned as the latter. But then later on when it was reorganised it was designated as the 4th Company, the 1st Platoon of the 2nd Battalion. Which means later on and throughout the rest of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, could you check whether the question as recorded reflects exactly what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. In fact, I'd asked whether at some point it had gone from being the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade and then became the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Smbr.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's what I heard and since the witness referred to the 2nd Battalion as well I think there is no confusion as far as the witness is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, we'll see some documents that reflect this. But let me ask you now: Despite the change in the designation of the battalion and the brigade the 4th Company reported to, there was no change in the composition of your platoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think the same personnel remained. Our platoons were there. So for the most part it remained understanding changed, at least in our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you just referred to "company," so that may -- you may have answered my next question which is: No change in the composition of your company resulted from the change in the designation of battalion and brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Everything remained as it was. It remained the same for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 30890.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, while we're waiting for this document to come up on the screen, let me explain a little bit about what it is. It's from the command - and now you can see it, you can see in the upper left-hand corner - it's from the command of the 3rd Battalion. It's dated 26 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We see at the bottom in B/C/S and the second page in English we see that it's signed by the commander Aleksandar Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now Aleksandar Petrovic, he's also known as Aco Petrovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We see here that Major Dragutin Lancaric [phoen] is appointed the commander of the 4th Company. Now this is the major you were just speaking of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we see that Sergeant Ljubomir Bozic is appointed as deputy. And among other appointments, we see that you are appointed commander of the 1st Platoon and we see that Lieutenant Dusan Zurovac is appointed the company supplies officer. Now, just a point of clarification, you've told us that you became platoon commander in the summer of 1992. Is that when you became platoon commander or is that in February of 1993 -- in fact, the 26th of February, 1993, as this document shows?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when Vito was wounded then I was there right away to replace him. But perhaps this order came later on. But I was the commander as of 1992. It is possible that this order was dated later, that it was send later. Vito was there, he was the commander at first, but then he was wounded and he was sent for treatment and then I took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and before we leave this document, again we see that it says the 3rd Battalion but I think we've -- we understand now that that doesn't -- if we later see a reference to 2nd Battalion we will not be confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please tender this document, Mr. President. It's 30890.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30890 receives number P6621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6621 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I wouldn't mind if you still participate in the proceedings when evidence is admitted, et cetera, and to listen to the next questions that are put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, on this document, now we've seen that Lieutenant Dusan Zurovac was the company supplies officer. He succeeded Major Lancaric as company commander at some point, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That was around late 1993 or early 1994, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I can't recall the exact date because these commanders were frequently replaced - company commanders, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This position, this position of company supplies officer, when you were platoon commander, that's the person at the company command that you would go to request or to receive supplies for your platoon; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was the company clerk, actually. Kept records of what was required and how. So that's what we called him, basically. He was called the company clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So some of the records he kept would be records of uniforms that were issued; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- he kept records of ammunition and weapons that were issued?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: He even kept records of cigarette rations; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now when the 1st Platoon received supplies, who would sign for it? Would that be you as the platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was there, yes. But if I wasn't, then there would be someone who would be standing in for me so that's how it usually worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that someone standing in for you, of course, that's from your platoon?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course. There was also the squad commander. He would stand in for me if I was on leave or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 30885.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, this document is headed -- well, we'll wait for the English to come up. Mr. Tusevljak, you can see that this document is headed: "4th Company of the 3rd Battalion, list of names of soldiers." So this would be before it became the 2nd Battalion. Now, on the first page of both, we see that your name as the 1st Platoon commander appears. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And on the second page of the English and the bottom of the first page of the B/C/S, under the heading "Wounded," you see the name Vitomir Kapuran and that is the full name of Vito; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 30885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30885 receives number P6622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Having clarified these matters, I'd like to turn briefly to your platoon's zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for that if I could please have the document that is now D541 brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Tusevljak, this is a map that you've made some marks on in a previous case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the bottom middle of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now at the bottom of this map in the centre, we can make out some faint writing in red. You placed the S to indicate VRS held territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the M indicates ABiH territory? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that faint red line we see between the M and the S, that is a line of disengagement where the line of confrontation -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now if we look just right of the area with the M and the S --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I would ask if we could zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I'll be focusing just above the 90 of that bottom margin and a little to the right of it. Here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you want to do with it later, but could we move it slightly so that the scale is visible as well which --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move a little bit to the left because I only need the last 200 metres from the 1 kilometre. Yes, that will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's perfect. I think that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We see just above the 90 and to the right, Mr. Tusevljak, we see the word "Ozrenska"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. And that marks -- yes, you've already answered my question, then. Okay. Now, I'm going to turn back for the next few questions to your statement for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So we don't need that map anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, yesterday you made a correction to paragraph 4 of your statement for this case so that it no longer includes the phrase "it was not possible to hit a tram from the Metalka building." When asked about this, you told Defence counsel that "it has nothing to do with me"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Indeed, this topic of hitting a tram from the Metalka building, that never comes up in your Karadzic statement or your Karadzic evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It is somewhere in Grbavica and I wasn't down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. It has nothing to do with you, so you knew immediately upon reading that sentence that it had nothing to do with you; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you knew when you were giving this statement that it might be used in legal proceedings before this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you understood the need to be truthful and accurate to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This statement for this case is one and a half pages. You've confirmed that that's your signature on this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if we could please have that brought up, now. That's D539.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask you now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But we can -- I'm sorry. I'll wait a moment until it's come up on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, this is one and a half pages. Did you read this statement over before putting your signature on this statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed it -- let me see, I can't recall the exact date. But this interview was on the days that are mentioned there, but I believe I signed it sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Mr. Tusevljak, where were you when you reviewed this statement and then signed it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean this signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I do mean this signature right here. Is there another signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the interview was earlier on. And at the time when I signed this I was in Budva. I work there in Montenegro. So I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who gave you this statement when you were in Budva in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly who of the Defence counsel was there, but I believe it was sent by mail to me and then I signed it and returned it to The Hague address.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, you've explained to this Court that you knew immediately upon looking at the reference to the tram and the Metalka building that it had nothing to do with you. Did you note that problem when you reviewed the statement before putting your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I signed the statement but I believed -- I thought that as previously when I was at the Karadzic trial, this could be corrected, you see, because the Defence counsel wasn't there present so I couldn't correct it right then and there. I sent it by mail and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I didn't sign this in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's be clear about something here: You did see that that was incorrect; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it down there quickly because I was working, so I had to go to copy it and I simply signed it thinking that I could correct it once I came here, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So it's clear that you signed it even knowing that it had something that you say had nothing to do with you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it. Again, I repeat that my intention was to correct it here. I didn't think that it was that important. I thought it would be corrected later. It has nothing to do with Metalka. It was far from my positions. I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you did not think it was important to sign a statement that you knew was materially incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I had nothing to do with it. I thought it was a mistake, typed there by error, and the attorneys probably know that I had nothing to do with the Metalka building. I thought that that was there inserted by error and that it's something that could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How would the attorneys know that that was incorrect and had nothing to do with you? Did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did tell them, yes. I have it here in my statement. I submitted a copy of the statement. I underlined that as something that would need to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we do note that the witness has some documents with him. And if the Defence do not object, we would request to review them at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber would like to first have a look at it before --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the witness apparently has a statement with him. Any problem if the Prosecution would inspect it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I don't know what it is, but no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Could you please give what you have in front of you to the usher so that we could have a look at it and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you were telling us --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll pause a moment, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you were telling us that you told the lawyers that it needed to be corrected. When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at The Hague, when I had a conversation with them, when I received this statement. I think that was the day before yesterday. The day before yesterday, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So between the 10th of May and the day before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Shin, we are close to the point anyhow where we take a break. Mr. Stojanovic, you have no idea what that is? No. Let me -- let's first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you said, I don't know what the witness has in front of him. It seems to be his statement. But quite a lot of other documents apparently relevant to this case, with a kind of a typewritten cover page. Is that totally unknown to you? You have no idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that I've seen now that these are documents that I used during the proofing of this witness here in The Hague. It's the same as the copy that I have that lists all the documents and perhaps three other documents that I found during the investigation which I asked -- which I was wondering whether I should include in the witness's -- in the documents that go with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic repeat the last half of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I've seen are all documents that I tendered in this case and that I went through with the witness in the proofing. I showed all the documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apparently you also gave a copy to the witness, is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I provided a copy to the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it true that there was one report of an investigation among those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you're thinking when you say report of an investigation. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw at the end the type of a report, of course I can't read it because it's in B/C/S, but it looked a bit as if it was a report about a specific event. I saw a few maps. But I also saw something which looked very much as if it were a report. Is that -- it was pretty much at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is a report that I have in front of me, then that's a report by the security services centre in Sarajevo, signed by Simo Tusevljak. And while searching documents, I asked the witness during proofing if he knew anything about this document. He said no, so I didn't even go on to ask him anything else about it. There are two or three other documents like this in this particular bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if the witness -- is it -- it is about what security service centre in Sarajevo dealing with what event or what incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report of the 6th of October, 1992, from the Sarajevo security services about the number of crimes, the type of crimes, how many operative actions they undertook, signed by Mr. Tusevljak. But it turned out that that's not this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you then -- why did you then provide him with a copy of that report if he doesn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided the document so that he could prepare himself before we started to work, before the proofing. I then thought that the document was not even relevant for our case, so I didn't tender it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was why you left a copy with the witness. Why does he need to be in -- why does he need to have a document with him which is totally irrelevant to your case which he doesn't know anything about? Of course, I'm wondering what kind of materials you gave to the witness which contain information which he's not otherwise aware of. That is the gist of my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I gave him this set of documents to read, to acquaint himself with the documents before I started to talk with him. I wanted to go through the documents so that we could work more efficiently later. I mean, there is nothing of dispute there. If I'm not permitted to give any documents to the witness, all you need to do is to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it could have been relevant. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying the one, I'm not saying the other. I asked myself what the purpose is of giving the witness information on matters he doesn't know anything about. But we'll further consider this at a later stage. We'll first take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, the Chamber would like to put a few questions to the witness before we ask you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before Mr. Shin continues his cross-examination I'd like to look again at your statement, that is D539. And I only need the original on the screen, please. Oh, it's already on the screen. Yes, I have it. Last page, please. Witness, you told us that you signed this when you were where, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Budva. I work there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where is that exactly? And you said in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how did you receive the statement you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received it by e-mail on the e-mail address of the gentleman that I worked for. I copied it, I signed it, and then I sent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you send it. Did you do that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, myself. I did it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly -- so you had a print-out. You signed it. Could I ask you did you put the date on it yourself as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then what did you do to send it back? What was needed to be done to send it back by e-mail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a copy shop, so I made a copy, I gave it to them, and they sent it to an address in The Hague. In this copy shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They sent it to an address in The Hague, an e-mail address. What happened with the original, the one you signed yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kept it. I think that I have it here in the hotel or at home. I'm not sure. But I think I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you bring it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think it's at the hotel. I have some documents here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would then be the copy you received by e-mail which was printed out for you. You didn't print it out yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was done at the copy shop by the people who work there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said you received it through your employer. Is that true? The person to -- you are employed by someone in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Budva? And why didn't you send it back through your employer? Why did you go to a copy shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went with him because the copy shop is very close to his house. He went to show me where it was and I gave it to the people who work there, so that they could print it so that I could sign it so that it could be scanned and sent back to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you write down the e-mail address to which it was to be sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, usually people who are using an e-mail are -- using the e-mail system on their computers, they usually have a way to print out their mails and any attachments to it. So I'm still wondering why your employer who received that e-mail did not print it out himself? Why send you to a copy shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That young man just had a telephone. So he received that on his phone. He didn't have a printer to be able to copy it. That's why we had to go to this shop, copy shop that was close by that had the option to print it and then send it back to this e-mail address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Had you given the e-mail address of your employer to whom so that they could send it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the gentleman who works at the copy shop who sent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I mean, when you received the statement through your employer, had you given the e-mail address of your employer? And if so, to whom did you give it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I was called by the Defence attorney and I gave him the address of my employer. I don't remember which attorney it was but it was one of the attorneys, and I gave him the address to which he could send the document. It was my employer's e-mail address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know by heart your employer's e-mail address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the name. I think it's Racanovic, that's the surname. I think his first name is Jovo. He lives in Budva. He had the phone and the address. I didn't have my own e-mail address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But were you able to give the e-mail address to the attorney who called you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the telephone. It was a telephone conversation. So that's how I sent the address of the employer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said you know his name. But a name in itself is not sufficient to send an e-mail. Did you have any additional information, and where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The employer gave me his e-mail address. I think there's a dot there. I think that the code was his date of birth. He gave it to me. I asked him if he had an e-mail address, he said he did, so he allowed me to use his address so that I could give it to the lawyer so that the lawyer could send the document to me. I don't remember this date, though. I don't remember the exact address. But his name was Racanovic, Jovo. He was a young man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do I therefore understand that you had two telephone conversations with the attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. When he called me, I said that I was in Budva, that I was working, that I couldn't come to Sarajevo. And then he said if I have an address he could call me -- he would call me again so that I could give him this address so that he could send this to me to this address so that I could sign it. Then he gave me the address of the lawyer here in The Hague to whom I could send this signed paper, or wherever the lawyer was. But anyway, it was his e-mail address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did sign it using your own pen or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I took my pen with me. I knew the lawyer would call me. I didn't know exactly at what time, so I had a pen handy and I signed -- so that I could sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But when you called him, you didn't have the copy of your statement there yet, isn't it? Because he first called you, then you said you couldn't come, then you got the e-mail address from your employer, he called you again and said that he would send it to that e-mail address. Now, was that all done in one day or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was that all done on the day you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that he called me the day before and then the next day we went to sign it. I always had a piece of paper and a pen with me so that I could write down the address -- actually, I had noted down the address of the employer so that when I got a call from the lawyer I would be able to tell him to which address he could send the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do I understand that the signed copy was sent by e-mail but not from your employer's computer or phone but from the copy shop's computer or phone? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the computer of your employer was used only to receive the statement and not to send the signed statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you bring for us the signed statement once you've found it. You said most likely you have it in The Hague but perhaps it's at home. Could you please provide that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin -- well, yes, Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Two additional matters. When the copy shop printed the statement for you, how many pages did they print?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, but I think it was three, four, five pages. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were in the copy shop when you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I read it quickly and I signed it and I gave it to the gentleman to send it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said you read it quickly. And you saw that this sentence which had nothing to do with you was included in this statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that it was there. I had provided this statement earlier. I knew what was written. I had provided the statement earlier in Sarajevo to the attorneys, and here it was perhaps an additional thing or change in the statement. And I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you realised that one information contained in the statement was wrong; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that it didn't have anything to do with me. But I thought that it was a printing mistake and I could correct it when I came here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I thought then that it could be deleted from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why didn't you just strike it before signing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I was working at the time. Everything was being done very quickly. I had to come back to work. I think later I crossed it out. I think here in the hotel or something when I was reading it more carefully, that's when I did it and I told the attorney that it had nothing to do with me and that it would need to be deleted, the matter about Metalka. And, Your Honours, I saw also there some issues about which battalion it was. I underlined it. I think it was the 2nd Battalion, 4th Company, 1st Platoon. I underlined it. I wanted to see with the lawyer what this was about. So it's these two or three issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you still about the same matter about: Were you aware of incident F4, as your statement says, which is in the indictment against Mr. Mladic? Do you have any personal knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this F4 was discussed when I was testifying in the Karadzic trial. I think it was the same incident at that intersection. That's when I learned about it. Before that, I didn't even know that it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any person knowledge about that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't know that this happened at all until I came to the trial of President Karadzic and that's when there was discussion about it. Before that, I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Metalka building, as you said, had got nothing to do with you. Why did it enter into -- why did it arrive at the statement at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I assume when we talked with the lawyers in Sarajevo we were in a room in some premises in Spasovdanska Street. There were several witnesses. After I was done, another witness came in, then another witness, perhaps they had something to do with this Metalka. Maybe the lawyer simply made a mistake and put it in, but it has nothing to do with me. It was in Grbavica. I was never there at those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if I understood the Defence well, it is only the sentence "it is not possible to hit the tram from the Metalka building" which will be taken out. What then remains -- and I read it to you -- what then remains --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in your statement there remains: "A sniper as a type of weapon was not even needed in order to fire in this specific case, as it was possible to target this sector and fire at it with a regular automatic rifle." Could you explain to us exactly what you meant with that, specifically to fire from where to what if you say it's possible to do it with an ordinary rifle, a regular automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant here was that we didn't use snipers; we didn't need them. The lines were so close together, some 10 to 15 metres apart, so that we just used automatic rifles. We didn't see that place. You couldn't really see the place. The lines were so close together that snipers were not required, so we didn't have any snipers by establishment. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you say that you don't need a sniper rifle was even not needed in order to fire in this specific case, and you said it was possible to target this sector and fire at it with a regular automatic rifle, which suggests that you could hit the target with an automatic rifle. Now, to say that you couldn't even -- let me just check what you said exactly. You didn't see that place. How can you fire with an automatic -- regular automatic rifle if you don't see that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I say, Your Honours, you don't see that place, so I didn't mean that place. What I meant was the line in front of us which was some 10 to 15 metres apart. I wasn't thinking about that place at all. We don't see that place from our positions at all. It's impossible to see it, even a building. I had a photograph. We don't even see the building. We see much farther above the building. I was thinking of opening fire up to a range or the distance of 50 metres at those enemy lines. This is what I was thinking of. We didn't need snipers. We didn't have them because the lines of the enemy were so close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do I understand that you have no knowledge whatsoever about incident F4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as I said, I didn't know about it until I attended the trial of President Karadzic. And, as I said, we didn't even see that from our positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this line where I drew indicating that place on the map, our lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, in your statement given afterwards, the statement given to the Mladic Defence, you're still commenting on incident F4. How could you if you have no knowledge whatsoever to say anything about whether in that specific case you could hit the target with a regular automatic rifle, if you don't know where it happened, if you don't know from where the shot was fired? What is it that you make -- that you are confident to make these kind of statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I talked to the lawyers they explained to me about the incident. This was in Sarajevo. As I was looking at the map -- I was born there. I know the line. I went to school there, so I know how far it is but you cannot see it. And I know that if it's possible to see it from some other area, then it's possible to use an automatic rifle. This is just what I commented upon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we did know about it. The lawyers told us about what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were commenting on what you were told had happened, and on that basis and with your personal knowledge of the area you commented as you did in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now did they not also say something about the Metalka building which then resulted in you saying something about hitting a tram from the Metalka building? That -- apart from whether you withdraw it, but, of course, I am puzzled by why it ever entered your -- came into your statement. And on the basis of what you explained to us just a minute ago, I'm wondering and I'm asking you whether it was perhaps that the lawyers came up with the Metalka building and that you commented on it but that you are not confident now to keep that on the record and rather withdraw that? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. It's possible that we mentioned something. Perhaps the lawyer did mention Metalka but I don't remember that. I said I didn't know anything about it. It was not in my area of responsibility. All I know is that -- where the building is, but I don't know how it came about that this was in my statement. This was a completely different line. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Before I go to the documents, I have just one question, Mr. Tusevljak, to follow-up on His Honour Judge Fluegge's questions. Now, you were asked a short time ago whether you saw the statement. I think you've been clear that you saw this reference to the tram in Metalka before you signed this document, but you actually said: "Yes, I think that it was there." You don't think. You knew it was there and you saw it before you signed the statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it quickly, I saw that, but the lawyer was not there with me at the time so that I could correct it. As I said, I sent the address to The Hague thinking that this will be possible to correct when I came here before testifying, and I underlined it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a photocopy of the document. We can return these to the witness now. I would ask the witness -- I have some questions about it, actually. Maybe we can go do them right now. If the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- could please assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- original will be returned to the witness. Witness, you should consult that document only if asked permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, I would like you to return to the second page of the document that's in front of you? And I believe Your Honours have given you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- permission on this occasion to do that. Now, actually, the paper is in front of you, not on the screen. Now, the second page is a chart; correct? Yes. And you see on the right-hand side of it some handwriting; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- by hand here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could the usher please assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have a copy, so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could also use the old fashioned ELMO. Why not use the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just told that we still use the ELMO. I am sorry. I had not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- realised that was the case. So we can have the second page which is the first page of the chart, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, the chart is a horizontal document -- yes. We've got it right there. You see that handwriting, Mr. Tusevljak? We all see that handwriting. Whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting. I don't know who wrote this but it's not my handwriting. I didn't even read what's there on the table. It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it is in English. I'm going to ask you to read that handwriting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't think of the handwriting but I meant the table in English, the writing of Mladic's diary of the 27th of June, 1992, action on Hrasno and Asimovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And now that you see what text I'm pointing to, this handwriting, whose handwriting is that? Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not mine. I don't know. When I got the statement, it was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we will leave that for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have any questions. Could you tell us one thing: When did you receive this bundle of papers? When did you receive it?
